title: Instance Attributes
concept: Not shared by all objects -- each has its own data

content.code:
class Cat:
    def set_name(self, n):
        self.name = n

    def meow(self):
        print(f"{self.name} says Meow!")

cat1 = Cat()
cat1.set_name("Kitty")

cat2 = Cat()
cat2.set_name("Nabi")

cat1.meow()
cat2.meow()

steps.title: Class Definition (Cat)
steps.explanation:
**`class Cat:`**

Python executes code from top to bottom in order.
We define a class (cat blueprint) named `Cat`.

**Goal of this lesson**: In the previous lesson, we added attributes from **outside** the object like `my_dog.name = "Buddy"`. This time, we'll learn how to add attributes **inside a method using `self.attribute`**. This is far more organized and is the approach used in practice.

**Python internals**: When Python encounters `class Cat:`, it executes the class body to register the methods, then creates the `Cat` class object. This class will have two methods defined: `set_name` and `meow`.

**Why this order?** The class must be defined first so we can later add methods and create objects from the blueprint.

**Execution order**: Execute class Cat -> Begin class body execution -> Start registering Cat class -> line 2

steps.title: Method Definition (set_name)
steps.explanation:
**`def set_name(self, n):`**

**Method**: A function defined inside a class is called a **method**. It's almost the same as a regular function, but with one special rule.

**The self parameter -- The core of Python OOP!**
The **first parameter** of every instance method must be `self`.
- `self`: A reference pointing to **"myself (the object)"** that called the method
- When a method is called, Python **automatically** passes the calling object to `self`

**Python's automatic conversion (very important!):**
```python
cat1.set_name("Kitty")     # Code we write
  |
Cat.set_name(cat1, "Kitty") # Python's internal conversion
```
That is, `cat1` is automatically inserted into the `self` position!

**Why is self needed?** Because multiple objects share the same method code. `self` is needed to distinguish **which object** this method is currently operating on. cat1 and cat2 use the same `set_name` code, but since `self` differs, each produces different results.

**Note**: `self` is not a reserved word but a **convention**. You could change it to `this` or `me` and it would still work, but the Python community **always uses `self`**.

**Execution order**: Execute def set_name -> Create set_name function object -> Register in Cat class -> line 5

steps.title: Method Definition (meow)
steps.explanation:
**`def meow(self):`**

We define another method `meow`. This method implements the behavior of a cat making a sound.

**A method with only self**: `meow(self)` has no additional parameters beyond `self`. This means it operates using only **the object's own data (self.name)**, without needing any external data.

**Key point about the method body `print(f"{self.name} says Meow!")`**: It accesses the `name` attribute of the calling object via `self.name`. When cat1 calls it, it reads cat1's name; when cat2 calls it, it reads cat2's name. The same code producing **different results** is the beauty of OOP!

**Caution**: What if `meow()` is called before `set_name()`? Since `self.name` doesn't exist yet, an `AttributeError` would occur! To prevent this, it's better to initialize attributes in the `__init__` constructor (we'll learn this in the next lesson).

**Execution order**: Execute def meow -> Create meow function object -> Register in Cat class -> Cat class definition complete -> line 8

steps.title: Creating the First Object
steps.explanation:
**`cat1 = Cat()`**

Calling `Cat()` creates the **first Cat object (instance)**.

**What happens inside Python during object creation**:
1. `Cat.__new__(Cat)` is called -> Allocates **empty Cat object** space in memory (0x2000)
2. `Cat.__init__(new_object)` is called -> Initializes the object (no `__init__` exists, so only default initialization)
3. Returns the **reference (address 0x2000)** of the initialized object
4. The variable `cat1` receives and binds to this reference

**State of cat1 at this point**: It's a **blank object** with no attributes! `cat1.__dict__` is an empty dictionary `{}`. The `name` attribute doesn't exist yet -- it will be added when the `set_name()` method is called.

Analogy: A cat has been born with a blank name tag. Its name hasn't been decided yet.

**Why this order?** Objects can only be created after the class definition is complete.

**Execution order**: Call Cat() -> Create object 0x2000 via __new__ -> Assign reference 0x2000 to cat1 -> line 9

steps.title: Calling cat1.set_name
steps.explanation:
**`cat1.set_name("Kitty")`**

We call the `set_name` method on the `cat1` object. Python **automatically passes cat1 to self**.

**Python's automatic conversion (once more!):**
```python
cat1.set_name("Kitty")       # Code we write (1 argument)
  |
Cat.set_name(cat1, "Kitty")  # Python's internal conversion (2 arguments!)
```
We only passed 1 argument (`"Kitty"`), but Python internally puts `cat1` as the **first argument (self)** automatically!

**Parameter binding**:
- `self` = `cat1` (object at 0x2000) -- **automatically passed**
- `n` = `"Kitty"` -- **passed by us**

Analogy: It's like telling a delivery person (method) "Put this name tag (Kitty) on this cat (cat1)." The delivery person automatically knows which cat (self) to work on.

**Execution flow**: At this line, execution **jumps into the function body (line 3)**. When the method finishes, it returns here.

**Execution order**: line 9 -> Create cat1.set_name bound method -> Call -> Jump to line 3 -> self=cat1, n="Kitty"

pythonMemoryState.note: set_name called -> About to jump to line 3

steps.title: Executing set_name (cat1)
steps.explanation:
**`self.name = n`**

This line is the key code that creates an **instance attribute**! It adds a new attribute `name` to `self` (currently the cat1 object at 0x2000) and assigns the value of parameter `n`, which is `"Kitty"`.

**Instance attribute vs Class attribute**: Instance attributes are **individually owned** by each object. cat1's name and cat2's name (to be created later) are completely different variables. It's like student IDs with the same form -- each student writes their own name.

**Caution**: `self.name` and `name` are different! Using just `name` creates a local variable, while `self.name` permanently stores the value on the object. If you forget `self.`, the value disappears when the function ends!

pythonMemoryState.note: name attribute added only to cat1 object

steps.title: Creating the Second Object
steps.explanation:
**`cat2 = Cat()`**

Now we create a **second Cat object**. Every time `Cat()` is called, Python creates a **completely new object** in memory.

**Key concept -- Object independence**: cat1 (0x2000) and cat2 (0x3000) are **completely separate objects**. Although created from the same blueprint (Cat class), they have different memory addresses and independent internal data.

**Analogy**: Think of them as two dolls made in the same factory (Cat class). Putting a name tag on one doll (cat1.name = "Kitty") doesn't automatically put a name tag on the other.

**State of cat2 at this point**: `cat2.__dict__` is an empty dictionary `{}`! The name attribute added to cat1 has absolutely no effect on cat2. cat2 still has no name.

**Python internals**: Again `Cat.__new__(Cat)` -> allocate new memory (0x3000) -> default `__init__` (does nothing) -> bind reference 0x3000 to cat2. Each time `Cat()` is called, this process repeats and a new object is born.

**Why this order?** After the previous set_name method call completes and returns to line 10, the next line (line 11) executes in order.

**Execution order**: Call Cat() -> Create new object 0x3000 via __new__ -> Assign reference 0x3000 to cat2 -> line 12

pythonMemoryState.note: Second Cat object created (cat2 has no name yet)

steps.title: Calling cat2.set_name
steps.explanation:
**`cat2.set_name("Nabi")`**

This time we call the `set_name` method on the `cat2` object. Python performs the automatic conversion again.

**Python's automatic conversion:**
```python
cat2.set_name("Nabi")       # Code we write (1 argument)
  |
Cat.set_name(cat2, "Nabi")  # Python's internal conversion (2 arguments!)
```

**Parameter binding:**
- `self` = `cat2` (object at 0x3000) -- **automatically passed** (cat2, not cat1!)
- `n` = `"Nabi"` -- **passed by us**

**Same method, different self**: The **exact same code (line 3)** executes as when `cat1.set_name("Kitty")` was called. But this time, since self points to cat2, the result is stored on the cat2 object. This is why `self` is so important in OOP!

**Analogy**: Using the same name-tagging machine (set_name method), but this time tagging the second cat (cat2).

**Why this order?** After the second object is created, the next line executes in order.

**Execution order**: line 12 -> Create cat2.set_name bound method -> Call -> Jump to line 3 -> self=cat2, n="Nabi"

pythonMemoryState.note: set_name called -> About to jump to line 3

steps.title: Executing set_name (cat2)
steps.explanation:
**`self.name = n`**

The **exact same line of code** as before, but this time `self` points to cat2 (0x3000), so the result is different. It adds a `name` attribute to the cat2 object and assigns `"Nabi"`.

**Python internals**: This is equivalent to `cat2.__dict__['name'] = "Nabi"`. cat2's `__dict__` changes from `{}` to `{'name': 'Nabi'}`.

**Let's compare the state of both objects at this point:**
- cat1 (0x2000): `__dict__` = `{'name': 'Kitty'}` -- its own name
- cat2 (0x3000): `__dict__` = `{'name': 'Nabi'}` -- its own name
- Cat class: Has `set_name`, `meow` methods -- **code is shared**

**Key insight**: The method code (set_name) exists as **only one copy** in the Cat class, shared by all objects. But because `self` points to the calling object, the same code can store **independent data** in each object. Sharing code while separating data is the core principle of OOP!

**Analogy**: There's only one stamping machine (set_name) in the factory, but it stamps different dolls depending on which one you bring.

**Why does it work this way?** `self` points to the **object that called the method**. When cat2.set_name() is called, self becomes cat2.

**Execution order**: self.name = n -> Add name="Nabi" to cat2.__dict__ -> Function ends -> Return to line 14

pythonMemoryState.note: name attribute added only to cat2 (independent of cat1)

steps.title: Calling cat1.meow
steps.explanation:
**`cat1.meow()`**

We call the `meow` method on the `cat1` object. Now that both cats have their names set, the meow method can produce each cat's sound with their own name.

**Python's automatic conversion:**
```python
cat1.meow()       # Code we write (0 arguments)
  |
Cat.meow(cat1)    # Python's internal conversion (1 argument = self!)
```

**Parameter binding:**
- `self` = `cat1` (object at 0x2000) -- **automatically passed**

**Execution preview**: Inside the meow method, `self.name` will be read. Since self is cat1, it will read cat1's name, "Kitty". cat2's name "Nabi" is completely unrelated.

**Python's attribute lookup order**: When accessing `self.name`, Python first checks cat1's `__dict__`. It finds name in `{'name': 'Kitty'}` and returns "Kitty".

**Why this order?** After all objects' names are set, the next line executes in order.

**Execution order**: line 14 -> Create cat1.meow bound method -> Call -> Jump to line 6 -> self=cat1

pythonMemoryState.note: meow called -> About to jump to line 6

steps.title: Executing meow (cat1)
steps.explanation:
**`print(f"{self.name} says Meow!")`**

The meow method body executes. It accesses `self` (cat1)'s `name` attribute, combines it with an f-string, and prints the result.

**Let's follow the execution step by step:**
1. `self` -> cat1 object (0x2000)
2. `self.name` -> cat1.__dict__['name'] -> "Kitty"
3. f-string evaluation: `f"{self.name} says Meow!"` -> `"Kitty says Meow!"`
4. `print("Kitty says Meow!")` executes -> Output to screen!

**Why does "Kitty" appear?** Because self points to cat1 (0x2000), and cat1's `__dict__` contains `'name': 'Kitty'`. cat2's name "Nabi" lives in cat2 (0x3000)'s `__dict__`, so it's completely unrelated.

**f-string review**: `f"...{expression}..."` replaces the expression inside curly braces with its **evaluated result**. Here `{self.name}` is replaced with `"Kitty"`.

**This is the essence of OOP!** When cat1 calls the same meow code, it prints "Kitty says Meow!"; when cat2 calls it, "Nabi says Meow!". **One code, different results per object** -- this is the essence of object-oriented programming.

**Execution order**: Read self.name ("Kitty") -> Evaluate f-string -> Execute print -> meow function ends -> Return to line 15

steps.title: Calling cat2.meow
steps.explanation:
**`cat2.meow()`**

This time we call the `meow` method on the `cat2` object. In the previous step, cat1.meow() printed "Kitty says Meow!" -- what result will we get this time?

**Python's automatic conversion:**
```python
cat2.meow()       # Code we write
  |
Cat.meow(cat2)    # Python's internal conversion
```

**Parameter binding:**
- `self` = `cat2` (object at 0x3000) -- not cat1 (0x2000)!

**Let's predict**: Inside the meow method, `self.name` will be read. This time self is cat2, so it finds name in cat2's `__dict__` and reads "Nabi". Therefore the output will be "Nabi says Meow!".

**Key point**: `cat1.meow()` and `cat2.meow()` execute the **same function code (Cat.meow)**. The only difference is which object goes into self. Thanks to self, one piece of code can behave differently for different objects.

**Why this order?** After the previous cat1.meow() call completes, the next line executes in order.

**Execution order**: line 15 -> Create cat2.meow bound method -> Call -> Jump to line 6 -> self=cat2

pythonMemoryState.note: meow called -> About to jump to line 6

steps.title: Executing meow (cat2)
steps.explanation:
**`print(f"{self.name} says Meow!")`**

The key here is who `self` is.
In this call, `self = cat2`, so `self.name` is `"Nabi"`.
Therefore the output is `Nabi says Meow!`.

Key summary:
- Method code exists once in the class
- Data differs per instance
- `self` points to the current calling object, making the same code behave differently

**Analogy**: Even reading the same script, if the actor (instance) is different, the delivery changes.

Caution:
- If you don't set `name` beforehand, you may get an `AttributeError`

pythonMemoryState.note: Each object prints its own name

quiz.question: What happens if you don't include `self` as the first parameter of a method?
quiz.explanation: When a method is called, Python automatically passes the object itself as the first argument. If there's no parameter (`self`) to receive it, a TypeError occurs saying the argument count doesn't match.

misconceptions.correct: Actually, you can rename `self` to anything (`this`, `me`) and it will still work.
misconceptions.why:
However, it's a **strong convention** in the Python community, so you should always use `self`.
Not following this convention will make your code very hard for others to read.

keyTakeaway: The first parameter of a method is always `self`. Use `self.variable` to store each object's own data.
